insights.headline: You mark every major loss with a permanent rerouting of your physical path, and never call it grief.
insights.explanation: After your brother's death you stopped walking through the square where he was stabbed, and you frame it as errand-efficiency — you resolve everything in one trip. After Simone left you stopped using the faster terminal because it's where you put her on the bus, and you frame that one as a pastel preference. Same substitution, two decades apart, two different losses: logistics language standing in for something you don't name.

insights.would_predict: If asked directly about a place tied to a painful memory, you'll describe the avoidance in practical terms — traffic, convenience, a better food stall — before, if ever, naming what actually happened there.

insights.headline: You believe being visibly needy invites disaster, so you perform self-sufficiency even while under real strain.
insights.explanation: You told your supervisor 'everything's resolved' minutes after being held up at knifepoint, you give your pastor the same line whenever he asks if you need anything, and you close your account of exhaustion, grief, and financial strain with the identical phrase — even Bete mocks it now. The phrase repeats verbatim across three decades as a reflex, not a considered answer, while the surrounding facts (shaking hands, skipped meals, a decade of loss) say something else.

insights.would_predict: In a health or mental-health check-in, you'll minimize symptoms verbally even while describing behaviors that show real depletion — the words and the body will disagree.

insights.headline: You repeatedly cut your own money and food to cover someone else's unspoken need, and hide that you did it.
insights.explanation: You funded Simone secretly for eighteen months by letting the sofa be repossessed and letting your family think you sold it. You gave your whole paycheck to a stroke victim's family and ate cream crackers while telling Bete you'd already eaten. You kept adding to Bete's envelope through a tight month rather than opening it, and ate badly for three weeks instead. Three decades, three beneficiaries, one move: your own hunger is the first thing you cut, and you conceal it from the person it would most implicate you to tell.

insights.would_predict: In a budgeting conversation, you'll underreport your own basic expenses before you underreport money set aside for someone else's future.

insights.headline: You put yourself between danger and the most vulnerable person present, but you've never let anyone do that for you.
insights.explanation: On the bus you engineered the standoff so that if it went bad, it went bad at the front, specifically because three passengers were elderly. With Bete you walked her commute three times at different hours to route her around an eighty-meter unlit wall. In both cases you absorbed the risk calculation alone and told almost no one — you never told Bete about the robbery, and she still doesn't know about the commute-timing. Worth exploring whether you can receive this kind of protection from anyone, or only give it.

evidence.quote: if this goes bad it has to go bad at the front. Not back there.

insights.would_predict: When you're in danger, sick, or overwhelmed yourself, you won't tell the people closest to you until well after the fact, if at all.

insights.headline: You say you want the people you love to move toward freedom, then quietly act to keep them close, without naming the contradiction as it happens.
insights.explanation: You say you want Bete in Campinas where nobody spits at her, but when a funded exchange program appeared, you found a lot of reasons, and she never raised it again — you flag this yourself: 'I know exactly what I did and I did it anyway.' A similar shape appears earlier: at seventeen you obsessively recalculated the ambulance route that could have saved Wellington even though you had no way to act on it. In both cases your planning impulse activates hardest exactly where the outcome is one you cannot control and may want and not want at once.

insights.headline: Your core skill is staying functionally present inside acute danger or grief, and people specifically recruit you for this rather than you offering it.
insights.explanation: Brother Bené didn't ask about Simone — he showed up at 4am and put coffee in front of you. Your supervisor, after the knife incident, physically marked the moment with a hand on your neck and an order to rest, which you refused. In both cases someone else recognized you were in crisis and intervened on your behalf; you didn't ask for help yourself, but you're legible enough in your competence-under-strain that others feel compelled to step in.

insights.headline: Edilson marks every major loss or trauma with a permanent rerouting of his physical path, and never names the rerouting as grief.
insights.explanation: After his brother's death he stopped walking through the square where Wellington was stabbed, reframing it as errand-efficiency (E1: 'you resolve everything in one trip, you understand?'). After Simone left he stopped using the faster terminal because it's where he put her on the bus, reframing it as a pastel preference (E2: 'the Guarapiranga side has better connections for me... So I go the other way'). The same substitution — logistics language standing in for an unspoken wound — appears at two separate decades and two separate losses, suggesting a durable habit of converting grief into geography rather than a one-off coping moment.

evidence.quote: I don't go through that little square.

insights.would_predict: If asked directly about a place tied to a painful memory, he will describe the avoidance in practical terms (traffic, convenience, a better food stall) before, if ever, naming what actually happened there.

insights.headline: Edilson believes that being visibly needy invites disaster, so he performs self-sufficiency even while quietly under strain.
insights.explanation: He tells his supervisor 'no, no, everything's resolved' minutes after being held up at knifepoint (E4: L45), gives his pastor the same line every time he's asked if he needs anything (E3: L40-42, 'Everything's resolved. Praise God' — a phrase his own daughter now mocks), and closes his account of exhaustion, grief, and financial strain in E5 with the identical formula ('I say no, no, everything's resolved, praise God... And it is. I mean it is.'). The phrase recurs verbatim across three separate decades and contexts as an automatic reflex, not a considered response, even when the surrounding facts (shaking hands, skipped meals, a decade of loss) say otherwise.

insights.would_predict: In a health or mental-health check-in, he will minimize symptoms verbally even while describing behaviors (skipped meals, sitting on shaking hands, four hours of sleep) that show real depletion — the words and the body will disagree.

insights.headline: Edilson positions himself as the calm buffer between danger and the most vulnerable person present, across a robbery and his daughter's commute — but has never let anyone do that for him.
insights.explanation: On the bus he engineered the standoff so 'if this goes bad it has to go bad at the front. Not back there' specifically because three passengers were elderly (E4). With his daughter, he walked her commute three times at different hours to route her away from an eighty-meter unlit wall (E5: 'the avenue has a wall on one side for about eighty meters... So I told her, go the long way'). In both cases he absorbs the risk calculation alone and tells almost no one afterward — he never told Bete about the robbery (E4: 'I never told Bete. She was ten.') and did the commute-timing without her knowledge (E5: 'she still doesn't know this'). Worth exploring whether he can receive this kind of protective attention from anyone, or only give it.

He'd just say, Edilson, sit there, and put a coffee in front of me'); his supervisor, after the knife incident, physically marked the moment with a hand on his neck and an order to rest, which Edilson refused (E4: 'take tomorrow... no, no, everything's resolved'). insights.headline: Edilson believes a concrete, completable task is what stands between him and collapse, and reaches for one at the exact moment feeling becomes unbearable.

The same mechanism shows up procedurally rather than verbally in E4: immediately after being robbed at knifepoint, rather than processing the event he 'finished the whole line... Filled the paper,' completing his full shift and paperwork before his hands even began shaking on the ride home. The task-completion isn't just about caring for others (as in the core_values entries) — it is specifically his mechanism for regulating his own state.
